children.text: Degradation of metal via a natural electrochemical process.

is usually defined as the degradation of metals by a naturally occurring electrochemical process. The formation of rust on iron, tarnish on silver, and the blue-green patina that develops on copper are all examples of corrosion. The total cost of corrosion remediation in the United States is significant, with estimates in excess of half a trillion dollars a year.

Perhaps the most familiar example of corrosion is the formation of rust on iron. Iron rusts when it is exposed to oxygen and water. Rust formation involves the creation of a galvanic cell at an iron surface (see figure below). The relevant redox reactions are:

children.text: Corrosion can occur when a painted iron or steel surface is exposed to the environment by a scratch through the paint. A galvanic cell results that may be approximated by the simplified cell schematic Fe(

One way to keep iron from corroding is to paint it. The layer of paint prevents the water and oxygen necessary for rust formation from coming into contact with the iron. As long as the paint remains intact, the iron is protected from corrosion.

Other strategies include alloying the iron with other metals. For example, stainless steel is an alloy of iron containing a small amount of chromium. The chromium tends to collect near the surface, where it corrodes and forms a passivating oxide layer that protects the iron.
Iron (and other metals) may also be protected from corrosion by
A method of protecting iron or similar metals from corrosion by coating with a thin layer of more easily oxidized zinc.

, a process in which the metal to be protected is coated with a layer of zinc. Because zinc is more easily oxidized than iron, the underlying metal is protected from corrosion even if the zinc coating is broken. When the iron is exposed to oxygen and water, zinc serves as an anode and is oxidized instead of iron. (Oxygen is reduced at the iron, which serves as the cathode.)
Another important way to protect metal is to make it the cathode in a
An electrochemical cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction takes place; also called a voltaic cell.
An approach to preventing corrosion of a metal object by connecting it to a sacrificial anode composed of a more readily oxidized metal.

and can be used for metals other than just iron. For example, the rusting of underground iron storage tanks and pipes can be prevented or greatly reduced by connecting them to a more active metal such as zinc or magnesium, as shown in the image below. This method is also used to protect the metal parts in water heaters, boat hulls and motors, bridges, and more. The more active metals (lower reduction potential) are called
Electrode constructed from an easily oxidized metal, often magnesium or zinc, used to prevent corrosion of metal objects via cathodic protection.

because they get used up as they corrode (oxidize) at the anode. The metal being protected serves as the cathode for the reduction of oxygen in air, so it simply serves to conduct (but does not react with) the electrons being transferred. When the anodes are properly monitored and periodically replaced, the useful lifetime of the iron storage tank can be greatly extended.
